ec2.a: Resizable virtual servers (instances) in the cloud. You choose CPU, memory, storage and OS, and pay only while they run, instead of buying hardware up front.
An Amazon Machine Image is a template with the OS and software needed to launch an instance. Baking a custom AMI makes new instances boot ready to work, identical every time.

ec2.q: How are Linux On-Demand EC2 instances billed?
ec2.a: Per second (with a 60-second minimum) while running. Stopping an instance stops compute charges, but attached EBS volumes are still billed for storage.

ec2.q: What does a security group do for an EC2 instance?
ec2.a: It is a stateful virtual firewall at the instance level. You write allow rules only; return traffic for allowed connections is permitted automatically.

ec2.q: Why put EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer?
ec2.a: The group replaces unhealthy instances and adds or removes capacity with demand; the load balancer spreads traffic across AZs. Result: self-healing and elastic.

ec2.q: How much notice do you get before a Spot Instance is interrupted?
ec2.a: A two-minute interruption notice. Spot suits fault-tolerant, stateless or checkpointed work; diversify instance types to lower interruption risk.

ec2.q: Why should you require IMDSv2 on instances?
ec2.a: IMDSv2 uses session tokens obtained by a PUT request, which blocks many SSRF-style attacks that try to steal instance role credentials from the metadata service.

ec2.q: Cluster vs spread vs partition placement groups?
ec2.a: Cluster packs instances close for low-latency networking (HPC). Spread puts each on distinct hardware for isolation. Partition groups racks for big distributed systems like HDFS.

lambda.a: Serverless compute that runs your code in response to events. No servers to manage, it scales automatically, and you pay per request and per duration of execution.

lambda.q: What is the maximum timeout for a standard Lambda invocation?
lambda.a: 900 seconds (15 minutes). Longer jobs should be split into steps (e.g. Step Functions) or run on containers such as ECS/Fargate.
By number of requests plus duration, measured in GB-seconds (memory x time). Idle functions cost nothing, which makes it ideal for spiky or low traffic.

lambda.q: How does memory setting affect a Lambda function?
lambda.a: Memory ranges from 128 MB to 10,240 MB, and CPU is allocated in proportion to memory. More memory can finish faster and sometimes cost less overall.

lambda.q: What is the default Lambda concurrency quota per Region?
lambda.a: 1,000 concurrent executions per account per Region by default, shared by all functions. It can be raised; reserved concurrency guarantees capacity for one function.

lambda.q: What is a cold start and how can you reduce it?
lambda.a: The delay while Lambda creates a new execution environment. Provisioned concurrency keeps environments warm; SnapStart (e.g. Java) restores from a snapshot.

lambda.q: What are Lambda destinations for asynchronous invocations?
lambda.a: Routes the result of an async invocation to SQS, SNS, EventBridge or another function on success or failure, giving richer failure records than a plain DLQ.

lambda.q: Max synchronous invocation payload for Lambda?
lambda.a: 6 MB each for request and response (1 MB for async). Pass large data by reference, e.g. an S3 key, rather than inline in the event.

ecs.a: A fully managed container orchestration service. It places, runs and restarts containers for you and integrates with load balancers, IAM and CloudWatch.
A package of an application and its dependencies that runs the same everywhere. Containers start fast and share the host kernel, so they are lighter than VMs.
No additional charge for ECS; you pay for the compute it runs on (EC2 instances or Fargate vCPU and memory) and any other resources used.

ecs.q: Task definition vs service in ECS?
ecs.a: A task definition is a blueprint (image, CPU, memory, ports, roles). A service keeps a desired number of tasks running and replaces failed ones.

ecs.q: Task role vs task execution role?
ecs.a: The execution role lets ECS pull images and write logs. The task role gives your application code its own AWS permissions. Keep both least-privilege.
They define where tasks run (Fargate, Fargate Spot or Auto Scaling groups) and can split tasks across them by weight, managing cluster scaling for you.

ecs.q: Why use the deployment circuit breaker on an ECS service?
ecs.a: It detects when a rolling deployment keeps failing to reach steady state and can automatically roll back to the last working version, reducing outage time.

ecs.q: What does a blue/green deployment give an ECS service?
ecs.a: The new version runs alongside the old; traffic shifts only after it is healthy, and rollback is just shifting traffic back. Safer than in-place updates.

fargate.a: Serverless compute for containers. You define CPU and memory per task and Fargate runs it; no EC2 instances to patch, scale or right-size.

fargate.q: Which orchestrators can run on Fargate?
fargate.a: Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS. You keep the orchestrator's APIs, while Fargate supplies the underlying compute.
For the vCPU, memory and storage your tasks request, billed per second (1-minute minimum) from image pull until the task stops.

fargate.q: Which network mode do Fargate tasks use?
fargate.a: awsvpc: each task gets its own elastic network interface and private IP, so security groups apply per task, not per host.

fargate.q: How do you size a Fargate task?
fargate.a: Pick a supported vCPU and memory combination at the task level. Right-size from CloudWatch metrics, since you pay for what you request, not what you use.

fargate.q: Why run Fargate tasks in private subnets?
fargate.a: Tasks have no public IP; outbound goes via NAT or VPC endpoints. This shrinks the attack surface while a load balancer or API front door handles inbound.
Runs interruption-tolerant tasks on spare capacity at a discount. Tasks get a two-minute warning before being stopped, so use it for stateless or retryable work.

fargate.q: When might ECS on EC2 beat Fargate on cost?
fargate.a: Large, steady, well-packed workloads can be cheaper on EC2 with Savings Plans or Spot, at the cost of managing instances. Fargate wins on ops simplicity.

eks.a: A managed Kubernetes service. AWS runs and scales the Kubernetes control plane across multiple AZs; you run workloads with standard Kubernetes tooling.

eks.q: What is a pod in Kubernetes?
eks.a: The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers that share networking and storage and are scheduled together onto a node.
An hourly fee per cluster for the control plane, plus the compute you use (EC2 nodes or Fargate). Clusters on extended support pay a higher hourly fee.

eks.q: What are EKS managed node groups?
eks.a: EKS provisions and manages the EC2 worker nodes (in Auto Scaling groups) for you, including graceful node updates, so you handle less node lifecycle work.

eks.q: How do pods get AWS permissions securely on EKS?
eks.a: Use EKS Pod Identity or IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) so each workload gets its own scoped IAM role instead of sharing the node's role.
An open-source node autoscaler that launches right-sized EC2 capacity directly for pending pods and consolidates underused nodes to cut cost.

eks.q: How must EKS cluster version upgrades be done?
eks.a: One Kubernetes minor version at a time: control plane first, then nodes and add-ons. Check for deprecated APIs before each step.
An EKS option where AWS also manages compute, networking, storage and core add-ons for the cluster, reducing day-2 operations for Kubernetes fleets.

beanstalk.a: A service that deploys and runs web apps from uploaded code, provisioning EC2, load balancing, scaling and monitoring for you while you keep full control.
No additional charge for Beanstalk itself; you pay for the underlying resources it creates, such as EC2 instances and load balancers.
A combination of OS, language runtime, web server and Beanstalk components, e.g. Node.js, Python, Java or Docker, that your app runs on.

beanstalk.q: Application, version and environment in Beanstalk?
beanstalk.a: An application holds versions (labelled code bundles). An environment is the running set of resources hosting one version, e.g. staging or prod.
Web server environments serve HTTP traffic. Worker environments pull jobs from an SQS queue to run background tasks without blocking user requests.

beanstalk.q: Why choose an immutable deployment in Beanstalk?
beanstalk.a: It launches a fresh set of instances with the new version and swaps only when healthy, so a failed deploy never touches the running instances.

beanstalk.q: How do you do blue/green with Beanstalk?
beanstalk.a: Deploy to a separate environment, test it, then swap environment URLs (CNAME swap). Rollback is a swap back. Keep databases outside the environment.
.ebextensions config files customise resources and settings; .platform hooks run scripts at deployment stages on Amazon Linux 2+ platforms.

s3.a: Object storage: you store objects (files plus metadata) in buckets, addressed by a key. It scales without limits on the number of objects you can store.

s3.q: How durable is S3 designed to be?
s3.a: 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability, by storing data redundantly across multiple devices and, for most classes, at least three Availability Zones.

s3.q: What is the largest single object S3 can store?
s3.a: 5 TB. A single PUT can upload up to 5 GB; use multipart upload for larger objects (recommended above about 100 MB for speed and retries).

s3.q: How do S3 storage classes differ?
s3.a: They trade storage price against access cost and speed: Standard for hot data, Standard-IA for infrequent access, Glacier classes for archives. Intelligent-Tiering moves data for you.

s3.q: Why keep S3 Block Public Access turned on?
s3.a: It overrides any policy or ACL that would make data public, preventing accidental leaks. It is enabled by default for new buckets; serve public content via CloudFront.

s3.q: What do S3 Lifecycle rules do?
s3.a: They transition objects to cheaper classes or expire them after a set age, including old noncurrent versions, cutting cost without manual clean-up.
S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for PUTs and DELETEs of objects, so a read after a successful write returns the latest data automatically.

s3.q: What does S3 replication need, and what is it for?
s3.a: Versioning on source and destination buckets plus an IAM role. Cross-Region replication supports DR, compliance and lower latency; same-Region helps aggregate logs.

ebs.a: Block storage volumes that attach to EC2 instances like a network hard disk. Data persists independently of the instance's life.

ebs.q: Can an EBS volume be attached to an instance in another AZ?
ebs.a: No. A volume lives in one Availability Zone and attaches to instances in that AZ. To move it, snapshot it and create a new volume elsewhere.
By provisioned storage per GB-month, whether used or not, plus provisioned IOPS/throughput for some types, and snapshot storage.

ebs.q: What baseline performance does gp3 include?
ebs.a: 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any size, and you can provision more IOPS and throughput independently of capacity. Usually cheaper than gp2.
Point-in-time backups stored in S3 behind the scenes. They are incremental, so only changed blocks are saved after the first, lowering cost.

ebs.q: How can you automate EBS snapshot schedules?
ebs.a: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup create, retain and delete snapshots on a policy, so backups happen without scripts.
Uses KMS keys to encrypt data at rest, in transit to the instance, and in snapshots. Turn on encryption by default per Region so new volumes are always encrypted.
Lets one Provisioned IOPS (io1/io2) volume attach to several instances in the same AZ. Apps must use a cluster-aware file system to avoid corruption.

efs.a: A serverless, elastic shared file system using NFS. Many EC2 instances, containers or Lambda functions can read and write the same files at once.

efs.q: How is EFS different from EBS?
efs.a: EBS is block storage for one instance in one AZ (Multi-Attach aside). EFS is a shared file system accessible across AZs by many clients.
Pay for the storage you actually use per GB-month, with no capacity to provision, plus charges that depend on throughput mode and storage class access.
Standard, Infrequent Access (IA) and Archive. Lifecycle management moves files that are not accessed to cheaper classes automatically.

efs.q: How do clients reach EFS across AZs?
efs.a: Through mount targets created in each AZ's subnet. Instances mount via the nearest target; security groups control NFS access.
Application-specific entry points that enforce a POSIX user and root directory, so each app or tenant sees only its own part of the file system.
Elastic (scales automatically, pay per use, recommended for spiky loads), Provisioned (set a level) and Bursting (scales with stored size).

efs.q: When choose EFS One Zone over Regional?
efs.a: One Zone stores data in a single AZ for lower cost; fine for dev or easily recreated data. Regional stores across AZs for higher availability.

glue.a: A serverless data integration service to discover, prepare, move and combine data for analytics, ML and applications, with no clusters to manage.

glue.q: What is the AWS Glue Data Catalog?
glue.a: A central metadata store of databases and tables (schema, location, format). Athena, Redshift Spectrum and EMR use it to query data in S3.

glue.q: How are Glue ETL jobs billed?
glue.a: By data processing units (DPUs) consumed over time, so you pay only while jobs run. There is no charge for idle infrastructure.

glue.q: What does a Glue crawler do?
glue.a: Scans data stores such as S3, infers schemas and partitions, and creates or updates tables in the Data Catalog so data becomes queryable.

glue.q: What engine runs Glue ETL jobs?
glue.a: Serverless Apache Spark (Python or Scala), plus Python shell jobs for light tasks. Glue provisions and scales workers per job.
State that tracks data already processed, so reruns of a job handle only new data instead of reprocessing everything.

glue.q: Why write partitioned Parquet from Glue?
glue.a: Columnar, compressed files partitioned by common filters (e.g. date) let Athena and Spark skip data, making queries faster and cheaper.

glue.q: What is AWS Glue Data Quality?
glue.a: Rules (in DQDL) that measure and monitor data quality in the catalog or in ETL jobs, so bad data can be flagged or stopped before it lands.

athena.a: A serverless, interactive query service that analyses data directly in S3 using standard SQL. No servers or data loading needed.

athena.q: How is Athena SQL priced by default?
athena.a: Per amount of data scanned by each query. Scanning less data (compression, partitions, columnar formats) directly lowers cost.

athena.q: Where does Athena get table definitions?
athena.a: From the AWS Glue Data Catalog, which records each table's schema, format and S3 location.
Partitions (e.g. by year/month/day) let Athena read only matching folders when you filter on them, cutting both scan time and cost.
Separating users or teams: each can have its own query result location, encryption and per-query data-scan limits to control cost.

athena.q: What does CTAS do in Athena?
athena.a: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT writes query results as a new table, e.g. converting CSV to partitioned Parquet in one step for cheaper future queries.

athena.q: Why do Parquet/ORC formats reduce Athena cost?
athena.a: They are columnar and compressed, so Athena reads only the columns a query needs and skips row groups using statistics.
Uses data source connectors (running on Lambda) to query sources beyond S3, like DynamoDB or relational databases, and join them in SQL.

lakeformation.a: A service to centrally govern, secure and share data in an S3 data lake, managing fine-grained permissions on Data Catalog resources.
Instead of juggling many S3 bucket and IAM policies, admins grant database, table and column access in one place, audited consistently.

lakeformation.q: Does Lake Formation cost extra for permissions?
lakeformation.a: No additional charge for Lake Formation permissions; you pay for underlying services like S3, Glue and the engines that query data.

lakeformation.q: What does registering an S3 location do?
lakeformation.a: Tells Lake Formation to manage access to that path, so integrated engines get temporary credentials based on Lake Formation grants.

lakeformation.q: How do you restrict access to certain rows or columns?
lakeformation.a: Grant column-level permissions or create data filters for row- and cell-level security, so users see only what they are allowed to.
Tag-based access control: attach LF-Tags to databases, tables or columns and grant on tag expressions. Scales far better than per-table grants.

lakeformation.q: Which engines honour Lake Formation permissions?
lakeformation.a: Integrated services such as Athena, Redshift Spectrum, Amazon EMR and AWS Glue ETL enforce the grants when reading catalog tables.

lakeformation.q: How does Lake Formation share data across accounts?
lakeformation.a: Grant catalog resources to other accounts or an organisation (via AWS RAM). Consumers query in place without copying, enabling a data mesh.

dynamodb.a: A serverless NoSQL key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond performance at any scale. No servers, patching or capacity planning in on-demand mode.

dynamodb.q: What is the maximum size of a DynamoDB item?
dynamodb.a: 400 KB, including attribute names and values. Store large blobs in S3 and keep a pointer to them in the item.
On-demand bills per read/write request and scales instantly, great for unknown traffic. Provisioned sets capacity (with auto scaling) and suits steady, predictable loads.

dynamodb.q: Why does partition key choice matter?
dynamodb.a: DynamoDB spreads data across partitions by partition key hash. A high-cardinality key spreads traffic evenly; a skewed key creates hot partitions and throttling.
A GSI has a different partition key, can be added any time and has its own capacity. An LSI shares the partition key and must be created with the table.
An ordered change log of item modifications kept for 24 hours. Lambda can process it to trigger workflows, update aggregates or replicate data.

dynamodb.q: What does point-in-time recovery give you?
dynamodb.a: Continuous backups so you can restore a table to any second within the recovery window (up to 35 days), protecting against accidental writes or deletes.
Multi-Region, multi-active replicas of a table. Apps read and write locally in each Region for low latency and keep running if one Region is impaired.

rds.a: A managed relational database service. AWS handles provisioning, patching, backups and failover for engines like MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle and SQL Server.
A synchronously replicated standby in another AZ with automatic failover, improving availability during outages and maintenance. It is not a read-scaling tool.
Per instance hour by class, plus provisioned storage, I/O for some storage types, backup storage beyond the free amount, and data transfer.

rds.q: What are RDS read replicas for?
rds.a: Asynchronously replicated copies that serve read traffic, offloading the primary. They can be in other Regions and can be promoted to standalone.

rds.q: How long can automated RDS backups be kept?
rds.a: Backup retention can be set from 1 up to 35 days, enabling point-in-time restore to any second in that window into a new instance.

rds.q: How should apps store RDS database passwords?
rds.a: In AWS Secrets Manager (RDS can manage the master password there with rotation), or use IAM database authentication, never in code.

rds.q: What does RDS Proxy help with?
rds.a: Pools and shares database connections, smoothing connection storms (e.g. from Lambda) and reducing failover time for applications.

rds.q: What does Performance Insights / Database Insights show?
rds.a: Database load broken down by waits, SQL, hosts and users, so you can find which queries cause bottlenecks before scaling hardware.

aurora.a: A cloud-native relational database compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL, built on a distributed storage layer for higher throughput and availability.

aurora.q: How does Aurora store data durably?
aurora.a: The cluster volume keeps six copies of data across three Availability Zones, so it tolerates loss of storage nodes and even an AZ.

aurora.q: Does Aurora storage need to be pre-provisioned?
aurora.a: No. Aurora storage grows automatically as data is added, and you pay for what is used, so no capacity planning for disks.

aurora.q: Writer vs reader endpoint in Aurora?
aurora.a: The cluster (writer) endpoint points to the primary for writes. The reader endpoint load-balances connections across Aurora Replicas for reads.

aurora.q: How many Aurora Replicas can a cluster have?
aurora.a: Up to 15 Aurora Replicas sharing the same storage volume. They scale reads and act as failover targets for the writer.
Capacity measured in Aurora Capacity Units that scales up and down in fine-grained steps with load, suiting variable or unpredictable workloads.
Clones share storage copy-on-write, so creating a test copy of a large database is fast and cheap until data diverges.

aurora.q: What does Aurora Global Database provide?
aurora.a: One primary Region plus read-only secondary Regions replicated at the storage layer with typically sub-second lag, for local reads and cross-Region DR.

elasticache.a: A managed in-memory data store and cache compatible with Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached, serving reads in microseconds to milliseconds.

elasticache.q: Why put a cache in front of a database?
elasticache.a: Frequent reads are answered from memory, cutting latency and database load, so you can serve more users with a smaller database.
A deployment option that scales cache capacity automatically with no nodes to size, billed on data stored and compute used.

elasticache.q: What is the cache-aside (lazy loading) pattern?
elasticache.a: The app checks the cache first; on a miss it reads the database and writes the result to the cache. Only requested data is cached.

elasticache.q: Why set a TTL on cached items?
elasticache.a: A time to live expires stale entries automatically, bounding how out of date data can get and keeping memory for hot keys.

elasticache.q: What does cluster mode enabled give Valkey/Redis OSS?
elasticache.a: Data is sharded across multiple node groups, each with replicas, scaling memory and write throughput beyond a single primary.

elasticache.q: How do you make a Valkey/Redis OSS cache highly available?
elasticache.a: Use replicas in other AZs with Multi-AZ automatic failover, so a replica is promoted if the primary fails.

elasticache.q: Which Valkey/Redis data type suits a live leaderboard?
elasticache.a: Sorted sets: members are kept ordered by score, so rank and top-N queries are fast without sorting in the application.

redshift.a: A managed, columnar data warehouse for analytics (OLAP). It runs complex SQL across large datasets using massively parallel processing.

redshift.q: OLTP vs OLAP: where does Redshift fit?
redshift.a: OLAP. Redshift is for big analytical queries over history. Transactional apps with many small reads/writes belong in RDS, Aurora or DynamoDB.
Run the warehouse without managing clusters; capacity scales automatically and you pay for compute used while queries run, measured in RPU-hours.
Queries data in S3 directly from Redshift using external tables, joining lake data with warehouse tables without loading it.

redshift.q: How do you bulk-load data into Redshift efficiently?
redshift.a: The COPY command loads in parallel from S3 (and other sources). Split input into multiple compressed files to use all slices.
They decide how rows are spread across nodes (AUTO, EVEN, KEY, ALL). Co-locating join keys avoids shuffling data between nodes during queries.
They order data on disk so range filters can skip blocks using zone maps, speeding queries that filter on e.g. dates.

redshift.q: Why use materialized views in Redshift?
redshift.a: They store precomputed results of expensive queries and can refresh incrementally, giving dashboards fast answers at lower compute cost.

neptune.a: A managed graph database for highly connected data, storing nodes (vertices) and relationships (edges) and querying paths between them quickly.

neptune.q: When is a graph database a better fit?
neptune.a: When relationships are the point: social networks, fraud rings, recommendations, knowledge graphs. Multi-hop joins that strain SQL become simple traversals.
Yes, Neptune Serverless scales capacity automatically with demand, alongside provisioned instances for steady workloads.

neptune.q: Which query languages does Neptune support?
neptune.a: Apache TinkerPop Gremlin and openCypher for property graphs, and SPARQL for RDF graphs.

neptune.q: How does Neptune store data for durability?
neptune.a: Like Aurora, on a cluster volume replicated six ways across three AZs, with up to 15 read replicas for scaling reads.

neptune.q: How does a graph help fraud detection?
neptune.a: Fraudsters share devices, cards or addresses. Traversing links in real time reveals rings of related accounts that row-by-row checks miss.

neptune.q: Why keep Neptune in private subnets?
neptune.a: Neptune runs inside your VPC; restricting access with security groups and IAM auth keeps the graph unreachable from the internet.

neptune.q: What is Neptune Analytics used for with GenAI?
neptune.a: An analytics graph engine with vector search; it can back GraphRAG in Bedrock Knowledge Bases, linking entities to improve answer relevance.

vpc.a: A logically isolated virtual network in AWS where you define IP ranges, subnets, route tables and gateways for your resources.
Its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway. Private subnets have no such route, so their resources are not directly reachable from the internet.

vpc.q: Can a subnet span multiple Availability Zones?
vpc.a: No, each subnet lives in exactly one AZ. For high availability, create subnets in at least two AZs and spread resources across them.
Security groups are stateful, allow-only, and attach to resources. NACLs are stateless, support allow and deny, evaluate rules in order, and apply per subnet.

vpc.q: What does a NAT gateway do?
vpc.a: Lets resources in private subnets start outbound connections (e.g. for updates) while blocking unsolicited inbound traffic. It is billed hourly and per GB processed.

vpc.q: Why use gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB?
vpc.a: Traffic reaches S3/DynamoDB over the AWS network without an internet or NAT gateway. Gateway endpoints have no extra charge, saving NAT data costs.

vpc.q: How many IP addresses does AWS reserve in each subnet?
vpc.a: Five: the first four and the last address of the subnet CIDR (network, VPC router, DNS, future use, broadcast). Plan subnet sizes accordingly.
Peering is a one-to-one, non-transitive link. Transit Gateway is a hub that connects many VPCs and on-premises networks, simplifying routing at scale.

route53.a: It is a highly available DNS service that translates domain names into IP addresses, plus domain registration and health checking.
A container for the DNS records of one domain. Public zones answer internet queries; private zones answer only inside associated VPCs.
A monthly fee per hosted zone plus per-query charges; health checks and domains are extra. Alias queries to many AWS resources are free.

route53.q: Why use an alias record instead of a CNAME?
route53.a: Alias records can point the zone apex (example.com) at AWS resources like CloudFront or a load balancer, which CNAMEs cannot, and track IP changes.
Weighted (split traffic by ratio), latency (send to lowest-latency Region) and failover (active-passive). Also simple, geolocation, geoproximity, multivalue, IP-based.

route53.q: How do health checks enable DNS failover?
route53.a: Route 53 checks endpoints and, when the primary fails, stops returning it and answers with the secondary record instead.

route53.q: What does Route 53 DNSSEC signing protect against?
route53.a: It lets resolvers verify responses came from your zone unaltered, defending against DNS spoofing and cache poisoning.

route53.q: What does Route 53 Resolver provide for hybrid networks?
route53.a: Inbound and outbound endpoints with forwarding rules so VPCs and on-premises DNS can resolve each other's private names.

cloudfront.a: A content delivery network that caches content at edge locations worldwide, so users get responses from nearby with lower latency.

cloudfront.q: What is an origin in CloudFront?
cloudfront.a: The source of the original content, such as an S3 bucket, a load balancer, API Gateway or any HTTP server. Edges fetch from it on a cache miss.

cloudfront.q: Why does CloudFront often lower cost as well as latency?
cloudfront.a: Cache hits are served at the edge, reducing load and data transfer from origins. Data transfer from AWS origins to CloudFront is not charged.
Lets CloudFront sign requests to a private S3 bucket so the bucket stays non-public and only the distribution can read it. Recommended over legacy OAI.

cloudfront.q: How do you make new content appear before the TTL expires?
cloudfront.a: Create an invalidation for the paths, or better, version file names (app.v2.js) so each deploy uses new cache keys.

cloudfront.q: What do cache behaviours let you do?
cloudfront.a: Apply different origins, TTLs, cache policies and functions per path pattern, e.g. cache static assets for a long time but pass API paths straight through.
Both restrict private content. Signed URLs suit single files; signed cookies grant access to many files (e.g. a video library) without changing URLs.
CloudFront Functions are lightweight JavaScript for sub-millisecond header or URL tweaks at scale. Lambda@Edge handles heavier logic, network calls and origin events.

apigateway.a: A managed front door to create, publish, secure and monitor APIs at any scale, routing requests to Lambda, HTTP backends or AWS services.

apigateway.q: Which API types does API Gateway offer?
apigateway.a: REST APIs (feature-rich), HTTP APIs (simpler, lower cost, lower latency) and WebSocket APIs for two-way real-time communication.
Per million API calls received plus data transfer; WebSocket APIs also charge connection minutes. No minimum fees.

apigateway.q: What is a Lambda proxy integration?
apigateway.a: API Gateway passes the whole request to Lambda as an event and returns the function's response, keeping routing logic simple.

apigateway.q: Default account throttle limit per Region?
apigateway.a: 10,000 requests per second with a burst of 5,000 (lower in some newer Regions). It can be raised; use stage or usage plan throttles per client.

apigateway.q: How can you authorise API Gateway requests?
apigateway.a: IAM (SigV4), Cognito user pool or JWT authorizers, or Lambda authorizers for custom logic. Validate tokens at the edge, not in every function.

apigateway.q: What are usage plans and API keys for?
apigateway.a: REST API features to meter and throttle individual clients and set quotas. API keys identify clients but are not a replacement for authorization.

apigateway.q: What are stages and why use them?
apigateway.a: Named snapshots of a deployed API (dev, prod) with their own settings, variables, logging and throttles, enabling safe promotion and canaries.

sqs.a: A fully managed message queue. Producers send messages and consumers poll them later, decoupling components so one can fail or slow without breaking the other.
A managed publish/subscribe service. A message published to a topic is pushed to every subscriber, such as SQS queues, Lambda, HTTP endpoints, email or SMS.

sqs.q: How long does SQS keep messages?
sqs.a: 4 days by default, configurable from 60 seconds up to 14 days. Consumers must delete a message after processing it.
Standard gives nearly unlimited throughput with at-least-once delivery and best-effort order. FIFO preserves order per message group and removes duplicates.
After a consumer receives a message it is hidden (default 30 s, max 12 h). If not deleted in time it reappears for retry. Set it above your processing time.
A queue that receives messages that failed processing more than maxReceiveCount times, isolating poison messages for inspection and redrive.
ReceiveMessage waits up to 20 seconds for messages instead of returning empty, reducing empty responses and request cost.

sqs.q: What is the SNS-to-SQS fan-out pattern?
sqs.a: Publish once to an SNS topic subscribed by several SQS queues; each consumer gets its own durable copy and scales independently. Filter policies route subsets.

eventbridge.a: A serverless event bus that routes events from AWS services, SaaS apps and your code to targets using rules, enabling loosely coupled event-driven apps.
A router that receives events. Each account has a default bus for AWS service events; you can create custom buses for your own applications.
Pay per event published to custom or partner buses (AWS service events to the default bus are free), plus features like Pipes, Scheduler and replay.

eventbridge.q: What is an event pattern in a rule?
eventbridge.a: A JSON filter matching fields such as source and detail-type. Only matching events are sent to the rule's targets, like Lambda or SQS.
Creating cron, rate or one-time schedules that invoke many AWS targets, with time zones and retries, without running your own scheduler.
Connect a source (e.g. SQS, DynamoDB Streams, Kinesis) to a target point-to-point with optional filtering and enrichment, replacing glue code.
Archives keep events from a bus; replay resends them to rules later, useful for recovering from bugs or testing new consumers.
EventBridge offers rich content filtering, schema registry, SaaS sources and replay. SNS offers higher throughput and push to mobile, SMS and email.

iam.a: Identity and Access Management controls who is authenticated (signed in) and authorised (has permissions) to use AWS resources. There is no extra charge for IAM.

iam.q: Why should you not use the root user for daily tasks?
iam.a: Root has unrestricted access that cannot be limited by policies. Protect it with MFA, lock away its credentials and use it only for the few tasks that need it.
A user has long-term credentials for one person or app. A role is assumed to get temporary credentials, which is safer and preferred for workloads and humans alike.
Grant only the actions and resources needed for a task. Start small, then refine with IAM Access Analyzer and last-accessed data.

iam.q: How does IAM evaluate an allow vs an explicit deny?
iam.a: Everything is denied by default. An allow grants access, but any explicit deny in any applicable policy always wins.

iam.q: How is cross-account access usually granted?
iam.a: Create a role in the target account whose trust policy allows the other account's principals to assume it via STS, giving temporary credentials.
A managed policy that sets the maximum permissions an identity can have. Useful to let developers create roles without escalating privilege.

iam.q: Do Service Control Policies grant permissions?
iam.a: No. SCPs in AWS Organizations only set the maximum available permissions for accounts; identities still need IAM policies that allow actions.

cognito.a: Customer identity for your apps: sign-up, sign-in, MFA and social or enterprise federation, issuing standard tokens your backend can trust.
A user pool is a user directory that authenticates users and issues JWTs. An identity pool exchanges identities for temporary AWS credentials.

cognito.q: How is Cognito user pool usage priced?
cognito.a: Mainly by monthly active users, with feature plans (Lite, Essentials, Plus) that add capabilities like advanced security at higher tiers.

cognito.q: What tokens does a user pool issue?
cognito.a: An ID token (who the user is), an access token (what they can call) and a refresh token (to get new tokens without signing in again).

cognito.q: What is managed login in Cognito?
cognito.a: Hosted, customisable sign-in pages with OAuth 2.0/OIDC endpoints, so you get sign-up, sign-in and social login without building auth UI.

cognito.q: How do you protect an API with Cognito?
cognito.a: Use a Cognito user pool or JWT authorizer in API Gateway so tokens are validated (signature, expiry, audience) before your backend runs.

cognito.q: What are Cognito Lambda triggers for?
cognito.a: Custom logic at points in auth flows, such as pre sign-up validation, custom messages or adding claims before token generation.

cognito.q: How do identity pools map users to IAM roles?
cognito.a: Via default authenticated/unauthenticated roles, rules on token claims, or roles from the token. Scope policies with identity ID variables.

kms.a: A managed service to create and control cryptographic keys. It integrates with many AWS services to encrypt data at rest with keys you govern.

kms.q: Do KMS keys ever leave the service unencrypted?
kms.a: No. KMS key material is protected by FIPS-validated hardware security modules and never leaves them unencrypted; you call KMS APIs to use keys.
A monthly fee per customer managed key plus a per-request charge for API calls. AWS managed keys have no monthly fee.
Data is encrypted with a data key, and the data key is encrypted by a KMS key. Bulk data never goes to KMS, keeping encryption fast and scalable.

kms.q: Customer managed vs AWS managed keys?
kms.a: Customer managed keys give full control of policies, rotation and deletion. AWS managed keys are created and rotated by the service for you.
The resource policy that controls access to a KMS key. Every key has exactly one; without it granting access, IAM policies alone cannot use the key.

kms.q: What happens when you schedule a KMS key for deletion?
kms.a: It enters a waiting period (7 to 30 days) during which it cannot be used and can be cancelled. Deleted keys make their data unrecoverable.
Related keys in different Regions with the same key ID and material, so data encrypted in one Region can be decrypted in another without re-encrypting.

shield.a: A distributed denial of service floods an app with traffic from many sources to exhaust its resources and make it unavailable to real users.

shield.q: What does AWS Shield Standard cost?
shield.a: Nothing extra. It is automatically applied to all AWS customers and protects against common network and transport layer DDoS attacks.
A web application firewall that filters HTTP(S) requests with rules, blocking threats like SQL injection, cross-site scripting and bad bots.

shield.q: Where can you attach an AWS WAF web ACL?
shield.a: To resources such as CloudFront distributions, Application Load Balancers, API Gateway REST APIs, AppSync APIs and Cognito user pools.

shield.q: Why start with AWS Managed Rules?
shield.a: They are curated rule groups maintained by AWS for common threats (e.g. OWASP-style attacks, known bad IPs), giving protection without writing rules.

shield.q: What does a rate-based rule do?
shield.a: Counts requests per client key (such as IP) over a time window and blocks or challenges those above your threshold, limiting floods and scrapers.

shield.q: Why put CloudFront and Route 53 in front for DDoS resilience?
shield.a: Their globally distributed edge absorbs and filters attacks far from your origin, and they are covered by Shield. Keep the origin locked to CloudFront.
Enhanced detection, the Shield Response Team, attack visibility, automatic application-layer mitigation and cost protection for scaling during attacks.

guardduty.a: A managed threat detection service that continuously analyses logs and activity to find malicious or unauthorised behaviour. No agents needed for foundational sources.

guardduty.q: Which foundational data sources does GuardDuty analyse?
guardduty.a: AWS CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs and Route 53 Resolver DNS query logs, read directly by GuardDuty without you enabling them.

guardduty.q: Is there a free trial for GuardDuty?
guardduty.a: Yes, a 30-day free trial per account and Region; afterwards pricing depends on the volume of events and data analysed.
An alert describing a potential security issue with a type, severity and affected resource, e.g. an EC2 instance talking to a known crypto-mining domain.
Optional coverage such as S3 Protection, EKS Protection, Runtime Monitoring, Malware Protection, RDS Protection and Lambda Protection.

guardduty.q: How do you auto-respond to GuardDuty findings?
guardduty.a: Findings are sent to EventBridge; a rule can trigger Lambda or Step Functions to isolate an instance, revoke keys or notify the team.

guardduty.q: What does Malware Protection for S3 do?
guardduty.a: Scans newly uploaded objects in chosen buckets for malware and can tag results, so downstream processes skip or quarantine infected files.

guardduty.q: How do you run GuardDuty across an organisation?
guardduty.a: Designate a delegated administrator account in AWS Organizations to enable GuardDuty for all member accounts and see findings centrally.

cloudwatch.a: CloudWatch monitors performance: metrics, logs and alarms. CloudTrail audits activity: it records who made which API call, when and from where.
Watches a metric against a threshold and changes state (OK, ALARM, INSUFFICIENT_DATA), triggering actions like SNS notifications or Auto Scaling.

cloudwatch.q: What does CloudTrail Event history show by default?
cloudwatch.a: The last 90 days of management events in a Region, viewable at no charge. Create a trail to keep events longer in S3.
An interactive query language for log groups to search, filter, aggregate and visualise logs, charged by data scanned.

cloudwatch.q: Why set a retention period on log groups?
cloudwatch.a: By default logs are kept indefinitely. Setting retention deletes old logs automatically, controlling storage cost and meeting data policies.

cloudwatch.q: What does CloudWatch anomaly detection do?
cloudwatch.a: Builds a model of a metric's expected pattern (including daily/weekly cycles) so alarms fire on unusual behaviour rather than a fixed threshold.

cloudwatch.q: Why enable CloudTrail log file integrity validation?
cloudwatch.a: CloudTrail creates signed digest files so you can prove log files were not modified or deleted after delivery, important for audits.
A trail created in the management or delegated admin account that logs events for every account in the organisation to a central location.

bedrock.a: A fully managed service giving access to foundation models from Amazon and other providers through one API, so you build generative AI apps without managing infrastructure.

bedrock.q: What is a token in a foundation model?
bedrock.a: A chunk of text (roughly a word piece) the model reads or writes. On-demand Bedrock pricing is per input and output token, so shorter prompts cost less.

bedrock.q: Is your Bedrock prompt data used to train the base models?
bedrock.a: No. Bedrock does not use your prompts and completions to train AWS or third-party models, and does not share them with model providers.

bedrock.q: What do Bedrock Knowledge Bases do?
bedrock.a: Managed RAG: they ingest your documents, chunk and embed them into a vector store, then retrieve relevant passages to ground model answers with citations.
A consistent request format for chatting with any supported model, including tool use, so you can swap models without rewriting code.
Configurable safeguards: content filters, denied topics, word filters, sensitive information redaction and grounding checks, applied to inputs and outputs.

bedrock.q: Why run model evaluations in Bedrock?
bedrock.a: To compare models or prompts on your own dataset with automatic metrics, LLM-as-a-judge or human review, choosing on evidence, not hype.

bedrock.q: How does prompt caching cut cost and latency?
bedrock.a: It caches a repeated prompt prefix (e.g. long instructions or documents) so later requests reuse it, reducing input processing for supported models.

agentcore.a: An agentic platform to build, deploy and operate AI agents securely at scale with any framework and any model, without managing infrastructure.
Software that uses a model to reason, plan and take actions with tools to reach a goal, rather than only answering one prompt.
A managed agent loop: specify a model, system prompt and tools in one API call, and harness handles orchestration, tool execution and memory.

agentcore.q: How does AgentCore Runtime isolate sessions?
agentcore.a: Each user session runs in its own dedicated microVM with isolated compute, memory and filesystem, which is terminated and sanitised when the session ends.
Short-term keeps turn-by-turn context in a session. Long-term extracts insights such as preferences, facts and summaries that persist across sessions.
Converts APIs, Lambda functions and services into MCP-compatible tools, and connects existing MCP servers, exposing them to agents via one endpoint.

agentcore.q: What problem does AgentCore Identity solve?
agentcore.a: Agent authentication and access: it works with existing IdPs such as Cognito or Okta and manages credentials so agents act on users' behalf securely.

agentcore.q: How do Observability and Policy govern agent fleets?
agentcore.a: Observability traces each agent step via OpenTelemetry into CloudWatch. Policy intercepts Gateway tool calls with deterministic, Cedar-compatible rules.

sagemaker.a: A fully managed service to build, train and deploy machine learning models, with managed notebooks, training jobs and hosting.

sagemaker.q: Why does ML need training data?
sagemaker.a: A model learns patterns from examples. Its quality depends on having enough relevant, correctly labelled data that reflects real use.

sagemaker.q: How is SageMaker AI training billed?
sagemaker.a: By the instance type and time your training job runs, billed per second, so compute stops costing when the job finishes.

sagemaker.q: What is a SageMaker training job?
sagemaker.a: A managed run that pulls data from S3, trains on the chosen instances with a built-in algorithm or your container, then writes the model artifact to S3.

sagemaker.q: How can you cut SageMaker training cost?
sagemaker.a: Managed Spot Training uses spare EC2 capacity at a discount; add checkpoints to S3 so interrupted jobs resume instead of restarting.

sagemaker.q: Which inference options does SageMaker AI offer?
sagemaker.a: Real-time endpoints, serverless inference, asynchronous inference for large or slow requests, and batch transform for offline datasets.

sagemaker.q: What is SageMaker Model Monitor for?
sagemaker.a: It watches deployed endpoints for data and model quality drift against a baseline and alerts you when predictions may be degrading.

sagemaker.q: How do Pipelines and Model Registry enable MLOps?
sagemaker.a: Pipelines automate data prep, training and evaluation steps; the Model Registry versions models with approval status to gate deployments.

q.a: A family of generative AI assistants from AWS: Q Developer helps with building on AWS, and Q Business answers questions from company data.
A managed assistant that connects to enterprise data sources and answers questions, summarises and generates content based on that data.

q.q: Where can you use Q Developer besides the IDE?
q.a: In the AWS Management Console, AWS documentation and chat apps like Slack and Teams, to explain resources, costs and errors.

q.q: What happens to Q Developer IDE plugins?
q.a: AWS announced end of support for the IDE plugins and paid subscriptions on April 30, 2027, with Kiro as the successor. Console Q is unaffected.

q.q: How does Q Business get company knowledge?
q.a: Through built-in connectors to sources such as S3, SharePoint and Confluence, which index content for retrieval when users ask questions.

q.q: Why are Q Business answers permissions-aware?
q.a: It honours source access control lists, so users only get answers from documents they are already allowed to see. Identity is key to safe rollout.
Integrations that let the assistant take actions in third-party apps, such as creating a Jira ticket, from within the chat.

q.q: How can admins keep Q Business on-topic and safe?
q.a: Use admin controls and guardrails: block topics or phrases, restrict answers to enterprise data, and configure response scope.

rekognition.a: A managed computer vision service that analyses images and videos to detect objects, scenes, text, faces and unsafe content via simple APIs.
Labels such as 'Car' or 'Beach' with confidence scores (and bounding boxes for some), so apps can tag and search images automatically.

rekognition.q: How is Rekognition image analysis priced?
rekognition.a: Pay per image processed (and per minute for stored video), with no upfront commitment; volume tiers lower the price.

rekognition.q: How does Rekognition read images from S3?
rekognition.a: APIs accept an S3 object reference, so Rekognition reads it directly. The caller needs permission to read the object.
DetectModerationLabels returns labels for unsafe or inappropriate content with confidence, so you can flag, blur or route items to human review.
Start an async job (e.g. StartLabelDetection) on a video in S3; Rekognition notifies an SNS topic on completion and you fetch results.

rekognition.q: Does a face collection store the face images?
rekognition.a: No. It stores face feature vectors extracted from images, not the images themselves, for search and comparison.
When built-in labels miss your domain, e.g. your own product parts. Train a model on your labelled images to detect them.

textract.a: A machine learning service that extracts printed and handwritten text, tables and form data from scanned documents, beyond simple OCR.
Optical character recognition turns images of text into machine-readable text. Textract adds structure: which text is a table cell or form value.
Per page processed, with the price depending on the API features used (text only costs less than tables, forms or queries).

textract.q: What does AnalyzeDocument add over DetectDocumentText?
textract.a: Feature types such as TABLES, FORMS (key-value pairs), QUERIES, SIGNATURES and LAYOUT, returning structured relationships between blocks.
Ask natural language questions like 'What is the policy number?' and get the answer extracted, without knowing the document layout.

textract.q: How do you process multi-page PDFs?
textract.a: Use asynchronous operations (e.g. StartDocumentAnalysis) on documents in S3; Textract publishes completion to SNS and you page through results.
AnalyzeExpense for invoices and receipts, AnalyzeID for identity documents and AnalyzeLending for mortgage packages, with pre-trained fields.

textract.q: How do you add human review to Textract?
textract.a: Integrate Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) so low-confidence extractions are routed to human reviewers before downstream use.
